title: Distributed Discovery of News and Perceived Misinformation Exposure: A Cross-Continent Application of the Resilience to Online Disinformation Framework
screen_reason: Secondary analysis of the 2021 Reuters Institute Digital News Report survey (46 countries, N = 91,061) in which respondents were asked whether they had seen false or misleading information about listed topics in the last week. The paper reports the share answering yes for coronavirus (53.9%) and for politics (43.1%). These are shares of survey respondents reporting having encountered misinformation, i.e. RECALL estimates with a denominator, so the paper is eligible even though its aim is to model the antecedents of perceived exposure rather than to describe prevalence.

estimates.country: Forty-six countries in six continents (North America, South America, Europe, Asia, Africa and Australia); named in the text are Norway, Colombia, Denmark, Kenya, Japan, Nigeria, South Korea, Brazil, Finland, Bulgaria, South Africa, India, the UK, Germany, the Netherlands, Italy, Canada, Taiwan, Singapore
estimates.platform: Not platform-specific: the survey item asks whether the respondent has seen false or misleading information about the topic, without naming a source or platform (respondents are online news users surveyed by YouGov)
estimates.date: Fieldwork January to February 2021 (Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2021); the item asks about 'the last week'
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who say they have seen false or misleading information about coronavirus in the last week
estimates.value_raw: PME to information related to the COVID (Yes = 53.9%; Norway = 29.8% to Columbia = 72.3%)
estimates.denominator: 91,061 respondents from the 2021 Reuters Institute Digital News Report, pooled across forty-six countries; national samples administered online in native languages by YouGov and described as representative of the respective online populations (in India, Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa only of younger English speakers)
estimates.definition: Respondent answered yes to having seen false or misleading information about coronavirus (from the list Politics, Coronavirus, Other health issues, Celebrities, Immigration, Products and services, Climate change or the environment, Other) in the last week; no external verification of whether what they saw was actually false
estimates.misinfo_def: "we adopt the term 'PME' from Stubenvoll et al. (2021), which is defined as 'information that lacks facticity in the eyes of the individual, regardless of its actual facticity and the perceived intention behind its spread'"; earlier, "Misinformation entails false or incorrect information"
estimates.source_quote: Affirmative answers were summed to create binary measures that measured PME to information related to the COVID (Yes = 53.9%; Norway = 29.8% to Columbia = 72.3%) and politics (Yes = 43.1%; Denmark = 19.9% to Kenya = 63.4%).
estimates.page_loc: Method, Individual-Level Measures, Dependent Variables (Perceived Misinformation Exposure), p. 288
estimates.ground_truth_detail: No ground truth: the respondent alone judges whether what they saw was false or misleading. Single binary self-report item from the Reuters DNR 2021 questionnaire; the authors are explicit that PME 'can reflect personal experiences of actual misinformation or a subjective opinion that misinformation or "fake news" is prevalent in the media environment' and that 'PME is fundamentally different to actual exposure to misinformation'.
estimates.moderator_quote: Respondents from the DNR survey answered the following question: "Have you seen false or misleading information about any of the following topics, in the last week?" The answer choices included: Politics, Coronavirus, Other health issues, Celebrities, Immigration, Products and services, Climate change or the environment, and Other.
estimates.notes: The value is verbatim. Confidence is medium only because the sentence 'Affirmative answers were summed to create binary measures' leaves it slightly ambiguous whether the COVID measure is the 'Coronavirus' option alone or 'Coronavirus' combined with 'Other health issues'; the labelling ('PME to information related to the COVID') points to the Coronavirus option. Pooled across all 46 countries; the country extremes (Norway 29.8%, Colombia 72.3%) are reported but are the ends of the distribution rather than a country breakdown, so no per-country rows were created.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Per-country PME values: the text names only the minimum and maximum countries for each measure (COVID: Norway 29.8%, Colombia 72.3%; Politics: Denmark 19.9%, Kenya 63.4%). Full per-country descriptives are said to be in Supplemental Table A1, which is not in the text file. I deliberately did NOT create rows for the four named countries: they are selected as distribution extremes, not as a country breakdown, and entering only extremes would bias any pooled estimate. An adjudicator wanting country-level rows would need the supplement. (2) The literature review states '54 percent of online users in the United States claimed they had come across some form of online misinformation in the previous week' citing the 2021 Reuters DNR. This is a figure the paper cites from another source, so it is not extracted (R8), even though it comes from the same dataset family. (3) Non-misinformation shares not extracted because they are not misinformation prevalence: 58% came across news incidentally on social media, 24% used a search engine for news, 72% of respondents across forty countries came across news through distributed forms of discovery (cited from DNR 2020), country-level news sharing on social media (M = 33.1%, range 11% Japan to 56% South Africa/Nigeria), public service media reach (M = 46.7%, 11% Brazil to 77% Finland), populist vote share (M = 19.9%). (4) All regression coefficients, correlations and converted probabilities (e.g. 'a one-unit increase in incidental news equates to a 55-percent probability of PME-COVID') are model quantities, not descriptive shares, so they are not extracted. (5) Judgement call for an adjudicator: this is a secondary analysis of the Reuters DNR 2021, so the two rows may duplicate estimates entered from the DNR report itself or from other papers using the same wave - a possible double-count at synthesis, flagged here rather than resolved (I cannot check other records under the blindness rule).

rob.design: Secondary cross-sectional survey analysis. Frame: Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2021, online samples in 46 countries administered in native languages by YouGov between January and February 2021, described as representative of each country's online population - with the authors' own caveat that in India, Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa the samples represent only younger English speakers, and no response rate is reported. N = 91,061 individuals matched to country-level data from V-Dem (typically five country experts per indicator) and the Global Party Survey (~19 experts per liberal democracy). Outcome measurement: single self-report binary items on having seen false or misleading information in the last week, with no verification of actual exposure; the authors acknowledge the binary measures lack variance and that PME may differ from actual exposure. Analysis: generalized linear mixed models (lme4) with random intercepts and random slopes, country ICC 6-7%, Benjamini-Hochberg correction at a 5% false discovery rate. No inter-coder reliability applies (self-report instrument).
